newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton prices steady in Pakistan, up in India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton prices steady in Pakistan, up in India.

text.p: Cotton prices were steady in Pakistan in the week to Thursday amid low demand but recovered in India after falling earlier in the week, dealers in the two countries said.
Pakistani prices remained more or less steady in the week after rising earlier on moderate buying of good quality cotton, dealers in Karachi said.
Most spinners were well stocked while high domestic prices kept exporters out of the market.
"If there is no fresh demand, ginners may give in," dealer Mustafa Hussain said, adding that prices might fall in the next few sessions.

Mills were not buying in large lots owing to interest rates of at least 22 percent on cotton bought on credit, broker Adil Nasim said. "Apart from a few big mills, others were buying only to meet their daily needs."

Pakistan's state-run Cotton Export Corporation said the country's cotton output from the 1996/97 (July-June) crop had reached a provisional 8.398 million 375-lb bales by February 20, down from 9.433 million bales in the year-ago period.
Mills had bought 6.569 million bales, down from 6.930 million in the year-ago period, while exporters had picked up only 4,600 bales against 1.110 million last year.
A total of 1.824 million unsold bales were stocked at ginning factories, compared to 1.392 million bales in the year-ago period, the corporation said.

Government officials estimate Pakistan's total 1996/97 crop to be below nine million bales, less than earlier predictions of 10 million bales and the previous crop of 9.96 million bales, because of pest damage in the past few months, mainly in the main growing Punjab province.
In the kerb market on Thursday, the K-68 variety was traded at 2,375 rupees and the MNH-93 at 2,400 rupees per maund (37.32 kg), dealers said.

In India cotton prices fell early this week but recovered later, dealers said on Thursday.

Prices weakened in sluggish mill buying and improved arrivals after assembly elections in Punjab state in the first week of February, but bounced back on hopes that the government might allow more exports.
In spot deals, Bengal-deshi settled five rupees higher at 790/830 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) while Punjab saw-ginned settled 10/15 rupees higher at 1,425/1,640 rupees per maund.
Gujarat Kalyan (medium-staple) initially fell by 200/300 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) but bounced back by the same margin later to settle at 11,400/11,600 rupees per candy.

The Indian Cotton Advisory Board, at its meeting on Monday, raised the estimate for the 1996/97 (July/June) crop by 500,000 170-kg bales to 16 million bales. The government's annual Economic Survey this week estimated the 1996/97 crop at 14.3 million bales.
"Higher crop estimate after late rains in producing centres has created optimism among traders that the government may allow fresh exports," said Manubhai Amarsey, a leading dealer.
"So far in the current season the government has allowed export of 1.22 million bales and we are expecting permission for about 200,000/300,000 bales."

The Advisory Board has scaled down the mill consumption estimate in the current season to 13.60 million bales from the previous estimate of 14.10 million bales as major millers were seen switching to polyster fibre.
